title: Are Your People Trained Or Enabled?
author: Melissa Muth Martinez
summary: Muth Martinez draws a distinction most organizations blur: training is episodic, push-model, and foundational (decision-driven events), while enablement is continuous, pull-model, and context-embedded (person-reached resources at the moment of application). Both serve purposes, but training alone fails on personalization, scale, and dependency; learners forget 70 percent of content within 24 hours and 90 percent within a week without reinforcement. The prescription is integration: pair training awareness with enablement infrastructure (reference guides, templates, coaching, communities) deployed where the work happens. Organizations that shift from training-heavy to enablement-first reward self-directed problem-solving and measure behavior change rather than session attendance.
points: Training and enablement serve different functions: training builds awareness in concentrated sessions; enablement sustains capability with just-in-time resources in daily workflows.
Learners forget 70 to 90 percent of training content without reinforcement, yet most organizations treat training as a destination rather than as a catalyst for ongoing support.
Enablement requires an ecosystem of resources, tools, processes, and coaching that people reach into at the moment of application, not a reliance on formal events.
Training dependency teaches people to wait for official sessions rather than seek learning in daily work; enablement-first cultures reward problem-solving and self-directed learning.
The organization that pairs training (foundational knowledge) with enablement (point-of-use support and coaching) captures performance gains that training alone never delivers.
quotes: Organizations invest billions annually in developing their workforce, yet many struggle to translate learning investments into durable performance improvements. At the heart of this challenge rests a fundamental distinction that is often overlooked: the difference between training your people and enabling your people.

Good training asks the question: “What do people need to know and understand to be able to do their jobs more effectively?” It operates on a push model. The organization decides what, when, and how learning happens.

Enablement, by contrast, is continuous and context-embedded. It requires an ecosystem of resources, tools, processes, and support systems that help people perform effectively in their daily workflows. Enablement asks: “What do people need to succeed, and how can we provide it when they need it?
I tend to think of training like an fancy appetizer at an overpriced restaurant. I mean, we kind of need it to get going, but it’s not nearly enough to satisfy and sustain us.
The distinction between training and enablement matters not just because people want and need support in the moment, but because knowledge transfer alone rarely produces lasting behavioral change.

Training and learning industry professionals generally agree that learners are likely to forget approximately 70% of training content within 24 hours and up to 90% within a week. This is supported by the concept of the forgetting curve, first documented by psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus, which shows that without reinforcement, memory retention decays.

Training can promote dependency and even disempowerment, as people are adapted to leaning into a particular kind of person or setting for learning rather than seek it out in everyday moments. Enablement, on the other hand, empowers people to solve problems with greater autonomy.

The question isn’t whether to invest in training or enablement, but rather how to build enablement infrastructure that multiplies training’s impact and creates self-sustaining cultures of continuous learning and growth.” Archived from Honest Office (Substack) on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
